posts.post_title: Who is called the father of Microbiology?
posts.post_content: Who among the following is regarded as the father of Microbiology, credited with first observing microorganisms under a microscope?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Antony van Leeuwenhoek

Antony van Leeuwenhoek first observed microbes and is called the father of Microbiology.

Correct Option Explanation

A Dutch merchant, he ground his own lenses and observed bacteria, protozoa and yeasts, calling them animalcules in 1677.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Louis Pasteur (1861) disproved spontaneous generation and developed vaccines for rabies and anthrax.
  • Robert Koch gave the first proof of the Germ Theory of Disease using Bacillus anthracis in 1876.
  • Edward Jenner (1796) developed the smallpox vaccine using cowpox lesions from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes.
Know More
  • Leeuwenhoek's findings were published via the Royal Society of London.
  • He was elected a Society member in 1680.
  • His microscope gave about 300-400X magnification.
  • He described bacteria, protozoa and yeasts, but not viruses.

posts.post_title: Who disproved the theory of spontaneous gene…
posts.post_content: The theory of spontaneous generation, which held that living beings arise from non-living matter, was conclusively disproved by which scientist using the swan-neck flask experiment?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Louis Pasteur

Louis Pasteur (1861) disproved spontaneous generation using his swan-neck flask experiment.

Correct Option Explanation

He used broths that allowed air in but kept out microbes, showing germs accumulated on the flask's cotton/neck rather than arising spontaneously.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Francesco Redi (1668) showed sealed jars of meat produced no maggots, disproving spontaneous generation of maggots, not microbes.
  • Spallanzani (1769) boiled and sealed broths, but Needham criticised his work, so the issue remained unresolved.
  • Virchow (1858) proposed the theory of biogenesis, that cells arise only from pre-existing cells.
Know More
  • Needham argued air was needed for spontaneous generation.
  • Pasteur's work supported the germ theory of disease.
  • Abiogenesis means life arising from non-living matter.
  • Biogenesis was later proved correct by Pasteur.

posts.post_title: Who first proposed the Germ Theory of Diseas…
posts.post_content: During the golden age of microbiology (1857-1914), the discovery that pathogenic microbes could be transmitted between surgical patients through unwashed hands and unsterilized instruments was demonstrated by whom?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Joseph Lister

Joseph Lister proved pathogenic microbes spread between patients via unwashed hands and unsterile instruments.

Correct Option Explanation

He introduced antiseptic surgery in 1867 by spraying carbolic acid on instruments and wounds, cutting surgical mortality.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Robert Koch gave formal proof of the germ theory with Bacillus anthracis in 1876, after Lister's surgical work.
  • Ignaz Semmelweis (1850) advocated handwashing to stop disease spread but predates Lister's antiseptic surgery.
  • Alexander Fleming discovered Penicillin in 1928, unrelated to germ theory's origin.
Know More
  • Lister also isolated a pure culture of Bacterium lactis.
  • Koch's postulates require the agent in every disease case.
  • Semmelweis worked in maternity wards before Lister.
  • Fleming's discovery led to the first antibiotic.

posts.post_title: Kochs postulates require the agent to be pre…
posts.post_content: According to Koch's postulates, which of the following criteria must be satisfied to establish a microorganism as the causative agent of a disease?

_aimcq_options.text: Only severe cases of the disease
Only chronic cases of the disease
Only fatal cases of the disease

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Every case of the disease

Koch's postulates require the causative agent to be present in every case of the disease.

Correct Option Explanation

The agent must also be isolated in pure culture, reproduce the disease in a susceptible host, and be re-isolated from that host.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Restricting to severe cases ignores mild or subclinical cases where the agent is equally present.
  • Restricting to chronic cases excludes acute infections, contradicting the universal presence criterion.
  • Restricting to fatal cases excludes recovered animals from which the agent is also recoverable.
Know More
  • Koch's postulates were formulated in 1882.
  • They were first applied to Bacillus anthracis.
  • Modern molecular postulates exist for unculturable agents.
  • Koch also developed solid media for bacterial growth.

posts.post_title: Petri dish was invented by
posts.post_content: The Petri dish, a fundamental tool for culturing microorganisms on solid media, was invented in 1887 by which scientist?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: R.J. Petri

R.J. Petri invented the Petri dish in 1887.

Correct Option Explanation

It provided a simple, reusable shallow dish for holding solid culture media, enabling isolation of colonies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Robert Koch pioneered growth of bacteria on solid media in 1881, a precursor development.
  • Christian Gram developed the Gram staining technique in 1884, unrelated to dish design.
  • Paul Ehrlich developed the acid-fast staining technique in 1882, not the Petri dish.
Know More
  • Petri worked as an assistant to Robert Koch.
  • Gram stain separates bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative.
  • Acid-fast staining is used for Mycobacterium species.
  • Solid media enable isolation of single bacterial colonies.

posts.post_title: Discovery of viruses is credited to
posts.post_content: In 1892, the discovery of viruses as filterable infectious agents smaller than bacteria was first reported by which scientist?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dmitri Ivanovski

Dmitri Ivanovski discovered viruses in 1892 while studying tobacco mosaic disease.

Correct Option Explanation

He found the infectious agent passed through filters that retained bacteria, indicating a new, smaller class of pathogens.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Martinus Beijerinck (1899) recognised that viruses depend on host cells to reproduce, building on Ivanovski's work.
  • Frederick Twort (1915) independently discovered bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, not viruses in general.
  • Felix d'Herelle (1917) rediscovered bacteriophages and coined the term "bacteriophage".
Know More
  • Ivanovski studied the tobacco mosaic virus.
  • Beijerinck termed the agent a "contagium vivum fluidum".
  • Bacteriophages mean "bacteria eaters".
  • Electron microscopes later allowed viruses to be visualised.

posts.post_title: Robert Koch discovered the causative organis…
posts.post_content: Which of the following diseases had its causative bacterial organism first discovered by Robert Koch in 1876?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Anthrax

Robert Koch discovered Bacillus anthracis, the cause of Anthrax, in 1876.

Correct Option Explanation

This was the first proof of the germ theory of disease, and Koch cultivated the organism outside the body using blood serum.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Typhoid's organism, Salmonella typhi, was discovered by Eberth in 1880.
  • Tetanus's organism, Clostridium tetani, was discovered by Nicolaier in 1885.
  • Plague's organism, Yersinia pestis, was discovered by Kitasato and Yersin in 1894.
Know More
  • Koch also formulated the four Koch's postulates.
  • Anthrax bacteria were cultured at body temperature.
  • Salmonella gallinarum causes fowl typhoid, discovered by Moore in 1895.
  • Brucella abortus (brucellosis) was discovered by Bang in 1897.

posts.post_title: Which field of microbiology studies fungi?
posts.post_content: Which specific branch of microbiology is concerned with the study of fungi?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mycology

Mycology is the branch of microbiology that studies fungi.

Correct Option Explanation

The term derives from Greek "myco", meaning a fungus, covering yeasts, moulds and their diseases.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Phycology studies algae (Greek "phyco", seaweed), a different microbial group.
  • Protozoology studies protozoa (Greek "proto", first; "zoo", animal), single-celled animals.
  • Bacteriology studies bacteria, prokaryotic single-celled organisms, distinct from fungi.
Know More
  • Virology is the study of viruses.
  • Divisions of microbiology include medical and veterinary microbiology.
  • Dairy microbiology studies microbes relevant to milk products.
  • Soil microbiology studies microorganisms in soil ecosystems.

posts.post_title: First rabies vaccination was given in the ye…
posts.post_content: In which year did Louis Pasteur administer the first successful rabies vaccination?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1885

The first rabies vaccination was administered by Louis Pasteur in 1885.

Correct Option Explanation

Pasteur had earlier developed attenuated vaccines for chicken cholera and anthrax before applying similar principles to rabies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1861 is when Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, not the rabies vaccine date.
  • 1882 is when Koch formulated his postulates, unrelated to the rabies vaccine.
  • 1928 is when Alexander Fleming discovered Penicillin, decades after the rabies vaccine.
Know More
  • Pasteur coined the term "vaccination" from Latin "vacca" (cow).
  • Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine used cowpox material.
  • Pasteur also solved the rancid-wine problem via pasteurization.
  • Attenuated vaccines use weakened, live pathogens.

posts.post_title: Complement fixation reaction was discovered…
posts.post_content: The complement fixation reaction, later applied in diagnostic serology, was discovered in 1900 by which pair of scientists?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou

Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou discovered the complement fixation reaction in 1900.

Correct Option Explanation

This immunological reaction later became the basis for serological diagnostic tests detecting antigen-antibody complexes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alexander Fleming discovered Penicillin in 1928, an antibiotic, not a serological test.
  • August von Wassermann (1906) introduced the complement fixation test specifically for syphilis, applying the earlier discovery.
  • Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope in 1931, unrelated to serology.
Know More
  • The Wasserman test diagnosed syphilis using complement fixation.
  • Complement fixation tests are used in veterinary serodiagnosis too.
  • Ernst Ruska's microscope allowed visualisation of viruses.
  • PCR was developed later by Kary Mullis in 1983.

posts.post_title: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by
posts.post_content: The system of binomial nomenclature, using two Latin names to identify each organism, was introduced in 1735 by whom?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carolus Linnaeus

Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature in 1735.

Correct Option Explanation

He grouped organisms into two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia, though single-celled organisms were not yet separately classified.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ernst Haeckel (1866) proposed a third kingdom, Protista, for single-celled organisms, after Linnaeus's system.
  • Herbert Copeland (1938) proposed a fourth kingdom, Monera, restricted to bacteria.
  • Robert Whittaker (1957) proposed a fifth kingdom, Fungi, separating them from plants.
Know More
  • Linnaeus's system used genus and species names.
  • Protista included amoebas, diatoms and some seaweeds.
  • Monera later became the Kingdom for prokaryotes.
  • Carl Woese later proposed the three-domain system in 1990.

posts.post_title: Who proposed the three-domain system of clas…
posts.post_content: Based on evidence from nucleic acid studies, the three-domain classification system comprising Archaea, Bacteria and Eucarya was proposed in 1990 by whom?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carl Woese

Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system, Archaea, Bacteria, Eucarya, in 1990.

Correct Option Explanation

The classification was based largely on differences in ribosomal RNA, revealing Archaea as molecularly distinct from Bacteria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Robert Whittaker (1957) proposed the five-kingdom system with Fungi as a separate kingdom, predating Woese's domains.
  • Ernst Haeckel (1866) proposed Protista as a third kingdom, a much earlier classification concept.
  • Herbert Copeland (1938) proposed Monera for bacteria, also predating the domain system.
Know More
  • Archaea live in extreme hot, saline or acidic environments.
  • Domain is a taxonomic rank above kingdom.
  • Woese's work used rRNA sequence comparisons.
  • Crenarchaeota and Euryarchaeota are kingdoms within Archaea.

posts.post_title: Bacteria are grouped under which domain?
posts.post_content: In Carl Woese's three-domain classification system, prokaryotic bacteria (excluding Archaea) fall under which domain?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacteria

True bacteria are placed in the domain Bacteria under Woese's three-domain system.

Correct Option Explanation

Archaea, though also prokaryotic, form a separate domain with distinct molecular and physiological traits from Bacteria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Archaea is a separate prokaryotic domain including methanogens and organisms living at high temperatures.
  • Eucarya is the domain for eukaryotic organisms such as protists, fungi, plants and animals.
  • Protista is a kingdom within domain Eucarya, not a domain itself.
Know More
  • Eucarya includes Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia kingdoms.
  • Archaea includes Crenarchaeota and Euryarchaeota kingdoms.
  • Bacteria diameter ranges roughly 0.5-1 micrometre.
  • High surface-area-to-volume ratio aids bacterial nutrient uptake.

posts.post_title: Comma-shaped bacteria with helical curvature…
posts.post_content: Bacteria that are helically curved rods, such as those seen in the genus Spirillum, are described by which shape term?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Spirilla

Helically curved rods are called spirilla (singular spirillum).

Correct Option Explanation

The name derives from the genus Spirillum; these are rigid, helically curved bacteria, unlike the flexible spirochetes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cocci are spherical bacteria, named from the Greek word for a berry.
  • Bacilli are straight rod-shaped bacteria, named from the Latin word for a stick.
  • Vibrio describes a comma-shaped bacillus with less than one complete twist, distinct from spirilla.
Know More
  • Spirochetes are highly flexible helical bacteria.
  • Cocci occur in arrangements like diplococci and streptococci.
  • Bacilli may occur singly, in pairs, or chains.
  • Length of spirochetes can reach up to 20 micrometres.

posts.post_title: Which bacterial arrangement produces grape-l…
posts.post_content: Cocci that divide in three planes in an irregular pattern, producing grape-like bunches, exhibit which arrangement?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Staphylococci

Staphylococci divide in three planes irregularly, forming grape-like bunches.

Correct Option Explanation

This irregular three-plane division distinguishes it from Sarcinae, which divide in three planes but in a regular, cuboidal pattern.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptococci divide in one plane, remaining attached to form chains, not clusters.
  • Diplococci divide in one plane and remain attached predominantly in pairs.
  • Sarcinae divide in three planes in a regular pattern, forming cuboidal arrangements, not irregular bunches.
Know More
  • Tetracocci divide in two planes forming groups of four.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is a classic staphylococcal example.
  • Streptococcus pyogenes forms chain arrangements.
  • Arrangement depends on plane of division and cell adhesion.

posts.post_title: Palisade arrangement of bacteria, like match…
posts.post_content: Which genus of bacteria characteristically shows a palisade arrangement, with cells lined up side by side like match sticks at angles to one another?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Corynebacterium

Corynebacterium shows the characteristic palisade arrangement of cells.

Correct Option Explanation

Cells line up side by side at angles, resembling a picket fence, a feature used in microscopic identification.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptococcus forms chains due to division in one plane, not a palisade pattern.
  • Bacillus subtilis forms chains of bacilli called streptobacilli, not palisades.
  • Saprospira forms trichomes, chain-like structures with high inter-cell contact, distinct from palisades.
Know More
  • Corynebacterium species include diphtheria-causing organisms.
  • Streptomyces forms branched filaments called hyphae.
  • A mycelium is a collection of hyphae.
  • Trichomes have more contact area between adjacent cells than chains.

posts.post_title: Bacteria classified as "very small" in size…
posts.post_content: Based on comparative bacterial cell size, which of the following genera is classified in the "very small" size category, alongside Chlamydia and Mycoplasma?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rickettsia

Rickettsia is classified among the "very small" bacteria, along with Chlamydia and Mycoplasma.

Correct Option Explanation

Bacterial size categories range from large (spirochetes, Bacillus) to very small (Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma), based on comparative dimensions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Escherichia coli falls in the "medium" size category, alongside Proteus.
  • Bacillus is classified as "large", alongside Spirochetes and Clostridium.
  • Spirochetes are also classified as "large" bacteria in this scheme.
Know More
  • Small bacteria include Brucella, Pasteurella and Haemophilus.
  • Cocci are approximately 1 micrometre in diameter.
  • Bacilli range 2-5 micrometres in length.
  • Rickettsia are obligate intracellular parasites.

posts.post_title: Which kingdom, proposed by Copeland, include…
posts.post_content: Herbert Copeland's 1938 classification proposed a distinct fourth kingdom exclusively for bacteria, called what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Monera

Herbert Copeland proposed Monera in 1938 to include only bacteria.

Correct Option Explanation

This separated bacteria from the broader Protista kingdom that Haeckel had earlier used for all single-celled organisms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Protista, proposed earlier by Haeckel, included all single-celled organisms including bacteria at the time.
  • Plantae covers plants (and originally fungi under Linnaeus), not bacteria.
  • Animalia covers animals, entirely unrelated to bacterial classification.
Know More
  • Whittaker's five-kingdom system retained Monera for bacteria.
  • Monera organisms are prokaryotic.
  • Protista under Whittaker's scheme covers only eukaryotic single cells.
  • Fungi became a separate kingdom under Whittaker in 1957.

posts.post_title: The protein subunit composing bacterial flag…
posts.post_content: Bacterial motility structures are hair-like helical appendages whose filament is composed of subunits of which protein?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Flagellin

The bacterial flagellar filament is composed of subunits of the protein flagellin.

Correct Option Explanation

Flagellin subunits arrange helically to form the flagellum's filament, one of its three parts along with the basal body and hook.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pilin is the protein monomer composing pili (fimbriae), not flagella.
  • Porin refers to outer-membrane channel proteins in Gram-negative bacteria, unrelated to flagella.
  • Murein is another name for peptidoglycan, the cell wall polymer, not a flagellar protein.
Know More
  • Flagella rotate like a corkscrew for bacterial motility.
  • Gram-negative bacteria have four basal body rings.
  • Gram-positive bacteria have only two basal rings.
  • Energy for flagellar rotation comes from proton motive force.

posts.post_title: A single polar flagellum arrangement is term…
posts.post_content: The flagellar arrangement in which a bacterium such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa possesses a single flagellum at one pole is called what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Monotrichous

A single polar flagellum arrangement, as in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is called monotrichous.

Correct Option Explanation

This is one of five flagellar arrangement patterns, distinguished by number and location of flagella on the bacterial cell.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lophotrichous describes a cluster of polar flagella, as in Pseudomonas fluorescens.
  • Amphitrichous describes flagella at both cell poles, as in Aquaspirillum serpens.
  • Peritrichous describes flagella surrounding the cell laterally, as in Salmonella typhi.
Know More
  • Atrichous bacteria have no flagella at all.
  • Flagellar diameter is about 0.01-0.02 micrometres.
  • Spirochetes move via periplasmic flagella (axial filaments).
  • Gliding motility occurs in Cytophaga without flagella.

posts.post_title: Pili (fimbriae) are composed of the protein
posts.post_content: Hollow, non-helical filamentous appendages called pili, involved mainly in bacterial attachment rather than motility, are composed of which protein monomer?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pilin

Pili (fimbriae) are composed of the protein monomer pilin.

Correct Option Explanation

Pili are shorter, thinner and more numerous than flagella, and mediate bacterial attachment to epithelial cell surfaces.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Flagellin is the protein subunit of the flagellar filament, used for motility, not attachment.
  • Porin refers to outer-membrane channel proteins, unrelated to pili structure.
  • Glutamic acid polymer composes the capsule of Bacillus anthracis, not pili.
Know More
  • Sex pili mediate DNA transfer during conjugation.
  • Pili help bacteria resist being washed away by mucus.
  • Pili occur in both motile and non-motile bacteria.
  • Flagella are involved in motility, unlike pili.

posts.post_title: Which structure is antiphagocytic and contri…
posts.post_content: A viscous glycocalyx layer surrounding certain bacterial cells, which inhibits engulfment by leukocytes and thereby contributes to virulence, is called what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Capsule

The capsule is antiphagocytic, inhibiting leukocyte engulfment and contributing to bacterial virulence.

Correct Option Explanation

Most capsules are polysaccharide-based; the anthrax capsule is unusually made of a polypeptide, a polymer of glutamic acid.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Flagellum is responsible for motility, not antiphagocytic protection.
  • Pilus mediates attachment and conjugation, not virulence via phagocytosis resistance.
  • Mesosome is an internal membrane invagination, unrelated to phagocytosis resistance.
Know More
  • Homopolysaccharide capsules are made of a single sugar type.
  • Heteropolysaccharide capsules contain many sugar types.
  • Bacillus anthracis capsule is a polyglutamic acid polymer.
  • Capsules also block bacteriophage attachment.

posts.post_title: A capsule too thin to see by light microscop…
posts.post_content: When a bacterial glycocalyx layer exists but is too thin to be visualised by ordinary light microscopy, it is specifically termed what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Microcapsule

A capsule too thin to be seen by light microscopy is called a microcapsule.

Correct Option Explanation

It differs from a true capsule (visible by special staining) but both are tightly bound, distinct from the loosely attached slime layer.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Slime layer is loosely associated with the cell and easily washed off, unlike a microcapsule.
  • Sheath is a hollow tube enclosing chains of cells in aquatic bacteria, a different structure.
  • Prostheca is a semi-rigid extension of the cell wall, unrelated to capsule thickness.
Know More
  • Capsules with definite boundaries are visible by special staining.
  • Slime layers can be easily removed by washing.
  • Sheaths may be strengthened by ferric or manganese hydroxides.
  • Stalks are non-living excreted appendages aiding attachment.

posts.post_title: Spirochetes exhibit swimming motility using
posts.post_content: Spirochetes lack external flagella yet still exhibit swimming motility, using a structure located beneath the outer cell envelope called what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Periplasmic flagella

Spirochetes swim using periplasmic flagella, located beneath the outer cell envelope.

Correct Option Explanation

These are also called axial filaments or endoflagella; they enable spirochetes to twist and contort their shape while swimming.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cilia are eukaryotic motility structures, not found in bacteria like spirochetes.
  • Pseudopodia are protoplasmic extensions used by amoebas for movement, not bacteria.
  • Pili are used for attachment and conjugation, not for swimming motility.
Know More
  • Spiroplasmas move without any motility organelle.
  • Gliding motility occurs in Cytophaga on solid surfaces.
  • Periplasmic flagella are also called axial filaments.
  • Spirochete motility mechanism is not fully understood.

posts.post_title: A cluster of polar flagella at one pole is c…
posts.post_content: The flagellar arrangement seen in Pseudomonas fluorescens, consisting of a cluster of flagella at a single pole of the cell, is termed what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lophotrichous

A cluster of flagella at one pole, as in Pseudomonas fluorescens, is called lophotrichous.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with monotrichous (single polar flagellum), where only one flagellum is present rather than a cluster.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Monotrichous refers to a single polar flagellum, as in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, not a cluster.
  • Amphitrichous refers to flagella at both poles, as in Aquaspirillum serpens.
  • Peritrichous refers to flagella surrounding the cell, as in Salmonella typhi.
Know More
  • Atrichous bacteria have no flagella.
  • Flagellar rotation resembles a corkscrew mechanism.
  • Basal body chemical composition is not fully known.
  • Hook and filament are made of helically arranged protein.

posts.post_title: Sheaths that enclose bacterial trichomes may…
posts.post_content: In some freshwater or marine bacteria, the hollow tube-like sheath enclosing chains (trichomes) of cells may be strengthened by impregnation with which compounds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ferric or manganese hydroxides

Bacterial sheaths may be strengthened by impregnation with ferric or manganese hydroxides.

Correct Option Explanation

This mineral impregnation reinforces the hollow tube that encloses trichomes (chains of cells) in some aquatic bacteria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Calcium dipicolinate contributes to heat resistance in bacterial endospores, not sheaths.
  • Peptidoglycan is the rigid cell-wall polymer, structurally unrelated to the sheath.
  • Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, not the sheath.
Know More
  • Prosthecae are semi-rigid extensions of the cell wall.
  • Stalks are non-living, excreted appendages for attachment.
  • Trichomes have high area of contact between cells.
  • Sheathed bacteria are common in freshwater and marine habitats.

posts.post_title: Sex pili are primarily involved in
posts.post_content: In bacterial genetics, sex pili play a specific functional role distinct from ordinary pili. What is that role?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Conjugation

Sex pili are involved in conjugation, the transfer of DNA between bacterial cells.

Correct Option Explanation

They act as tubules connecting donor (F+) and recipient (F-) cells, allowing plasmid or chromosomal DNA transfer.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Attachment to epithelial cells is the role of ordinary pili (fimbriae), not sex pili specifically.
  • Motility is provided by flagella, not pili of any type.
  • Sporulation is a distinct process forming endospores, unrelated to pili function.
Know More
  • F+ cells possess the fertility (sex) factor.
  • F- cells lack the fertility factor.
  • Conjugation can transfer large DNA fragments.
  • The F factor is an example of an episome.

posts.post_title: Homopolysaccharide capsules are synthesized
posts.post_content: Capsules made of a single type of sugar, called homopolysaccharides, are synthesized by which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Outside the cell from disaccharides by extracellular enzymes
Inside the cell and secreted as finished polymer

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Outside the cell from disaccharides by extracellular enzymes

Homopolysaccharide capsules are synthesized outside the cell from disaccharides by extracellular enzymes.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with heteropolysaccharide capsules, which are synthesized from sugar precursors activated inside the cell, then transported out.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "Inside the cell and secreted as finished polymer" better describes heteropolysaccharide capsule synthesis, not homopolysaccharide.
  • "By the nuclear material" is incorrect; capsule synthesis involves enzymatic, not genetic material, action directly.
  • "Within the cytoplasmic membrane only" omits the extracellular enzymatic step characteristic of homopolysaccharide synthesis.
Know More
  • Most bacterial capsules are polysaccharide-based.
  • Bacillus anthracis capsule is a polypeptide exception.
  • Capsules increase suspension stability via charge repulsion.
  • Capsules protect bacteria from desiccation by binding water.

posts.post_title: Cytophaga species exhibit which type of moti…
posts.post_content: Cytophaga species move only when in contact with a solid surface, showing a slow, sinuous flexing motion. What is this motility type called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gliding motility

Cytophaga species exhibit gliding motility, requiring contact with a solid surface.

Correct Option Explanation

The mechanism is not fully understood; movement is slow, only a few micrometres per second, with a sinuous flexing motion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Swimming motility occurs in liquid via flagella (or periplasmic flagella in spirochetes), unlike surface-dependent gliding.
  • Twitching via pili is a different surface-associated movement mechanism not described for Cytophaga here.
  • Flagellar motility requires flagella, which Cytophaga's gliding motility does not use.
Know More
  • Gliding motility is slow, a few micrometres per second.
  • Spirochetes swim via periplasmic flagella instead.
  • Bacteria with polar flagella swim back and forth.
  • Peritrichous bacteria tumble when flagellar bundles fly apart.

posts.post_title: Which bacterial genus shows terminal endospo…
posts.post_content: The endospore is positioned terminally and can be so large that it distends the cell, a feature typical of which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium tetani

Clostridium tetani typically shows terminal endospores that distend the cell, giving a drumstick appearance.

Correct Option Explanation

This is distinct from Bacillus cereus (central spore) and Bacillus subtilis (subterminal spore) locations.

posts.post_title: Negative-sense RNA viruses with segmented ge…

Correct Answer: For varying periods after clinical recovery

Convalescent carriers shed the pathogen for varying periods after clinical recovery from disease.

Correct Option Explanation

This shedding period may range from weeks to months, making such animals an important, sometimes overlooked, source of ongoing infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "Only during the initial incubation period, before any symptoms" describes animals in incubation, a different carrier category from convalescent carriers.
  • "Continuously from birth without any recovery phase" does not match the definition, which specifically follows clinical recovery.
  • "Exclusively through vertical transmission to offspring" describes a transmission route, not the convalescent carrier shedding pattern itself.
Know More
  • Shedding period may range from weeks to months.
  • Animals in incubation may also excrete the pathogen.
  • Contact carriers acquire pathogens without developing disease.
  • Both carrier types can silently spread infection.

posts.post_content: Among physical mutagens affecting bacterial DNA, which one is specifically described as causing breaks in the phosphodiester backbone of the nucleic acid?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: X-rays

X-rays are described as causing breaks in the phosphodiester backbone of nucleic acid.

Correct Option Explanation

This differs mechanistically from UV light, which instead causes cross-linking dimers between adjacent pyrimidine bases, especially thymine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • UV light causes pyrimidine dimer cross-linking, a distinct damage mechanism from the backbone breaks caused by X-rays.
  • Base analogues cause mutation by substituting for normal bases during replication, not by breaking the backbone.
  • Intercalating agents distort DNA structure to cause replication errors, a different mechanism from direct backbone breakage.
Know More
  • UV light causes thymine dimer cross-linking specifically.
  • Base analogues include 5-bromouracil as an example.
  • Intercalating agents include acridine orange and proflavin.
  • Both UV and X-rays are physical mutagen categories.

posts.post_title: The disadvantage of the direct microscopic c…
posts.post_content: The direct microscopic count method, using a Petroff-Hausser chamber, offers rapid counting with minimal equipment. What is cited as a key disadvantage of this method?

_aimcq_options.text: It cannot distinguish whether counted cells are alive
It requires expensive electronic particle counters
It can only be performed on solid agar media
It takes several days to yield any results

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: It cannot distinguish whether counted cells are alive

A key disadvantage of direct microscopic counting is that it cannot distinguish whether the counted cells are alive.

Correct Option Explanation

This applies similarly to electronic enumeration, since both methods count all cell-sized particles without assessing viability.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • "It requires expensive electronic particle counters" is incorrect; the Petroff-Hausser chamber is a simple, non-electronic slide-based method.
  • "It can only be performed on solid agar media" is incorrect; direct microscopic counting uses a liquid bacterial suspension, not agar.
  • "It takes several days to yield any results" is incorrect; direct microscopic count can be made rapidly with minimal equipment.
Know More
  • Petroff-Hausser chamber squares are 1/400 mm² in area.
  • Plate counts, by contrast, only count viable (living) cells.
  • Electronic counters also cannot distinguish live from dead cells.
  • Direct counting also allows morphology observation.
